🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.44% (intraday, 7-year +21bp). At trading day 13 (last close) it was -1.62% against a five-campaign average of -0.37% at the same point — 1994-95, 2022-23 were worse. The spread leg adds -0.35%. The 10-year is +26bp since the hike vs a +6bp campaign average at the same point.
  • HY Contagion: Junk-bond stress: the CCC-to-single-B spread gap is 696bp against a five-year average of 408bp (widest since Apr 2020). Better-rated junk is following: single-B +42bp and BB +34bp in a month. CCC and single-B are moving together more (correlation 0.28 → 0.49 over 3 months; five-year norm 0.70). Investment grade is untouched (+2bp).
  • Stocks: Big US stocks rose about half a percent; small companies fell.
  • FX: The dollar eased slightly; the yen stays weak near 158 per dollar.
  • Technicals: S&P and Nasdaq are far above their usual trend lines and look stretched.
  • Sectors: Utilities led today; tech still leads the month while banks lag.
  • Credit/Spreads: Most bond risk premiums stay low, but the riskiest junk bonds keep worsening.
  • Crisis: Overall stress is moderate; high government borrowing costs are the biggest worry.
  • Inflation: Underlying inflation is slowly cooling, but too many prices still rise fast.
  • Tech Bubble: Valuations are well below 2000 extremes, but easy credit looks late-cycle.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Delta reports Thursday and JPMorgan next Tuesday; Airtel Money lists in London.
  • Iran: We found no update after September 8; the Hormuz talks remained stuck then.
  • Warsh: Fed chair Warsh leans hawkish; a hike is possible, a cut unlikely.
  • Week Ahead: Big-bank earnings Tuesday; retail sales and producer prices Thursday.
  • Outlook: Lean neutral short-term: prices are stretched while weakness spreads in junk credit.
  • Trades: Cut the riskiest junk bonds and don't chase Nasdaq; buy only on pullbacks.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 sell, 24 hold long, 20 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.98 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 99th pctile, +2bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Big stocks look calm on the surface, but junk-bond stress is spreading.

PM close, Tue Oct 06. Large caps added to the rally. The S&P 500 rose 0.578599% to 7818.93 (+44.98), the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.4457496% to 27599.79 and the Dow rose 0.4942274% to 51521.28. The Russell 2000 fell 0.5914364% to 2830.297, so breadth is narrow and leadership is in mega caps. VIX slipped 0.51 to 15.01. Europe gained about half a percent (Euro Stoxx 50 6272.23, STOXX 600 636.63, FTSE 100 10541.69) and the Nikkei 225 led with +1.053829% to 70683.98. Bonds rallied: UST 10Y yields fell 2.53bp to 5.2793%, the 2Y fell to 4.7975% and Gilts fell 4.3bp to 5.375%. DXY eased 0.30% to 101.86. Brent rose 0.79 to 101.11. The biggest story is under the surface, in junk credit. Headline US HY OAS is 3.07% (17th percentile, computed) and IG is 0.82% (7th percentile, computed), both near cycle tights. But the Bloomberg Caa–B gap is 696bp against a 5y average of ~408bp. That is the 99.8th percentile of the last 5 years (computed) and the widest since 2020-04-28. Caa OAS is 992bp: +123bp over 1 month and +202bp over 3 months. FRED's CCC–B gap of 890bp sits at the 100th percentile of its history. Is the CCC stress spreading upward? Partly. Over the past month, single-B widened 42bp (to 296bp) and Ba widened 34bp (to 185bp), and the HY–IG gap rose 38bp. The B–Ba gap only rose 8bp, though, and is still below its 5y average (111bp vs ~129bp). So single-B and BB are moving roughly together rather than single-B breaking away. IG has barely moved (+2bp 1m, 82bp). The 63-day Caa/B correlation of daily changes rose to 0.49 from 0.33 a month ago and 0.28 three months ago. That points to more co-movement, but it is still below its 5y median of 0.70. Read: lower-quality stress has spread from CCC into the B/BB tiers in level terms, but has not reached IG. This is a descriptive read, not a validated signal. Sentiment is complacent at the index level (low VIX, S&P z-score 2.9 vs its trend, computed) and deteriorating at the bottom of the credit ladder. Iran and the hawkish Warsh Fed remain the macro backdrop. Both are covered below, with the caveat that we could not verify any Iran development after September 8.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

Today (US 1d) was defensive-led. Utilities rose +3.01%, Real Estate +1.13% and Cons Staples +0.96%. That fits a lower-yield day, alongside Cons Discr +1.39%. Health Care (-0.16%) lagged. On a 1-month view, growth leads decisively: Info Tech is +6.85% and Comm Services +4.05%, while Financials are -6.9% and Real Estate -5.85%. Materials (-3.96%), Utilities (-3.9%) and Industrials (-1.92%) are all down over the month. Year to date, Energy (+39.32%) and Info Tech (+31.79%) dominate, while Utilities (-4.73%), Cons Discr (-2.39%) and Financials (-1.69%) are negative. Global sectors tell the same story: Info Tech is +39.43% YTD and +6.16% over 1 month, Financials are -6.06% over 1 month, and Materials -6.17% and Real Estate -7.05% over 1 month. Read: a narrow growth/tech-plus-energy market, with rate-sensitive and credit-sensitive groups (financials, real estate) under pressure. That pattern matches 10Y yields above 5.2% and widening lower-quality credit. Today's defensive bounce looks like a rates relief move, not yet a rotation.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.98 vol points (74th percentile of the 35 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 105.2 (76th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 113bp (steeper by 37bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (88bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.30 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🗞️Street View — Where the Cycle Is HeadingCURATED · AS OF 2026-10-01

Consensus is a short, shallow campaign: one or two more 25bp hikes, December more likely than October. The debate is whether hiking into an energy shock ends in recession, and the bond market is already doing some of the tightening.

The Fed

  • Sept 16: unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, the first since 2023. Dots: median one more hike in 2026; 16 of 18 see at least one, 4 see two. Inflation not back at 2% until 2029. (CNBC, FedAndMarkets)
  • Warsh's message was distinctly hawkish (inflation 'too high and broad-based'); the Conference Board calls it 'not a one and done'. (Conference Board)
  • Sept 29, Williams (NY Fed): 'no need for urgency'; one more hike 'late this year' may be appropriate; the biggest inflation shocks have passed. (Bloomberg, NY Fed)
  • Sept 30, August PCE came in soft: headline 3.4% (vs 3.7% expected), core 3.0% (vs 3.3%). October odds fell; December still priced. Kashkari: inflation 'still too high'. (CNBC, CNBC (Kashkari))

Market pricing

  • October 28 hike odds vary widely by venue, roughly 35% to 69% (prediction markets highest, CME futures ~58%), mostly measured before the soft PCE print. (PredictionMarketsPicks)
  • About 83% odds of another hike by year-end; futures price ~93bp of tightening over the next 9 meetings, more than the dots. (Forbes)

Bonds and credit

  • 10-year Treasury above 5.25% (Sept 28), the highest since 2007; 30-year ~5.49%. Drivers cited: sticky energy inflation (Iran war), heavy issuance, AI capex demand. Term premium ~1.0–1.4%. (CNBC, CNBC (Warsh's yield problem))
  • AI-related issuers trade ~115bp vs ~78bp for IG overall; high-yield AI supply $40B year to date vs $12B in all of 2025. BNP and Goldman warn the issuance could pressure spreads. (Reuters, Bloomberg (BNP))

The bear case

  • Rosenberg: the Fed has never hiked into an energy shock without a recession, and AI won't save it this time. (TheStreet)
  • Goldman called the case for hiking 'weak' (demand not overheating, energy inflation should fade when the war ends). Oxford Economics: 'The Fed cannot control energy prices'; the risk is a weaker labor market. (CNN)

Read-through: For bonds, the bigger risk is the long end, not the Fed: term premium and supply keeping the 10-year above 5% matter more than one extra 25bp. The recession call is loud but isn't in any sell-side house view yet.

Curated summary of published Fed, market and economist commentary (news and research via the web), not a computed series and not a forecast. Odds differ by venue and move daily.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (40x) ≈ 23% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Today's market has the plumbing of a bubble without the price tag of one. Financial conditions are loose: NFCI is -0.55, IG OAS is at the 7th percentile and VIX is 15 (computed). Margin debt is growing 33.7% YoY (46% of the way to the peak condition, computed). Semis trade at 45.46x, 64% of the way to the 2000-peak condition, which makes them this cycle's leadership excess. Nasdaq's aggregate trailing P/E of 39.75x is nowhere near the 175x 2000 peak, and the index is 11.4% above its 200DMA versus a 50% peak stretch. On the chart overlay anchored at the Oct-2022 low, the current path is at 251.2 after 48 months. That is above the dot-com path from its Oct-1990 anchor at month 48 (235.7) and below the 1994-reset path at month 48 (268.4) (computed). The 2000 peak came at month 113 and month 69 of those paths respectively. The yield curve is positively sloped at 48.18bp, and both ISM PMIs are in the mid-50s with only 9–10% rollover signal. The 2000 template ended with a -78.0% Nasdaq drawdown over 31 months. Today's warning lights are in credit and complacency, not valuation, so a CCC-led credit turn is the more relevant transmission channel than a P/E collapse. The five headline estimates (top-10 weight ~40%, CAPE ~39x, market cap/GDP ~215%, IPO froth 55, LT EPS-growth signpost 65) are analyst estimates not re-verified by web search this run. The IPO froth estimate draws on reports of record 2026 IPO proceeds and a possible Anthropic mega-listing.

⚔️Iran War

We could not verify any Iran-war development dated October 2026. The most recent sources we found run to early September (GlobalSecurity.org Day 193 update, Sept 8). At that point, no US or Israeli strike inside Iran had been confirmed since late August, which extended the pause on strikes on Iranian territory. A senior Iranian official told Reuters in August that Tehran was shifting to a 'fully offensive' posture because efforts to end the war were deadlocked. On Aug 25, Oman's foreign minister met Iran's foreign minister in Tehran. Their joint statement set out a phased framework: a temporary joint navigation corridor and joint mine-clearing in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran said it would not treat the strait as open until Washington met its commitments under the June MoU: lifting the naval blockade, dropping oil sanctions and releasing frozen assets. Market read (analyst inference): Brent at 101.11 says the market still prices a closed or impaired Hormuz. Any verified corridor opening is the biggest downside risk for oil and upside catalyst for bonds.

Sources: Iran War 2026 -- Day 193 Update (GlobalSecurity.org) · Iran War 2026 -- Day 181 Update (GlobalSecurity.org) · Iran War 2026 -- Day 180 Update (GlobalSecurity.org)

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Inference: hold at the Oct 28 FOMC with a hawkish bias, and a hike not ruled out. Coverage says markets priced about a 16% chance of a 25bp October hike after his testimony, and that he has kept the option of a 2026 hike open if inflation stays high.

~1 YEAR

Inference: policy stays restrictive for longer. Cuts are unlikely while core PCE is near 3% and flexible CPI is near 5%. Hikes are possible if inflation re-accelerates. Coverage also says he has signalled a review of the Fed's tools, which may mean balance-sheet changes rather than only rate changes. Easing would most likely come only after a clear credit or growth break.

On the record, per the cited coverage, Warsh has said inflation is not slowing and has reaffirmed bringing it back to 2%. At Jackson Hole in August he left the door open to a hike this year if inflation stays elevated. Coverage reports money markets lifted September-hike odds to ~60% from 36% after that speech, and puts the policy rate at 3.50–3.75% in the cited reports. We could not confirm the September decision itself, nor any October speech. Reading his record against today's data: core PCE at 3.00759, flexible CPI at 4.94 and wide price breadth argue for patience on cuts. A falling core trend and widening CCC spreads are what could eventually soften him. Several sources are secondary aggregators (cryptobriefing.com), so treat specific odds figures as reported, not verified.
